exercises.instruction: 9, 10, 11, and 12 The vector field $$\mathbf{F}$$ is shown in the $$xy$$ -plane and looks the same in all other horizontal planes. (In other words, $$\mathbf{F}$$ is independent of $$z$$ and its $$z$$ -component is $$0$$ .) Is $${div}\mathbf{F}$$ positive, negative, or zero at $$P$$ ? Explain. Determine whether $${curl}\mathbf{F} = 0$$ . If not, in which direction does $${curl}\mathbf{F}$$ point at $$P$$ ?

problem.paragraph: 9. Details A vector field and a point are graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The vectors point vertically upward. The arrows are longer near the x-axis and become shorter as we move vertically upward. A point labeled P is placed approximately at the center of the field. Negative $${curl}\mathbf{F} = 0$$

10. Details A vector field and a point are graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. There are four rows of four vectors each. The vectors in the first row, just above the x axis are horizontal. The vectors in the second row point up and to the right. The vectors in the third and fourth rows progressively lean more toward the right. The arrows are shorter near the origin and become longer as we move away from the origin in all directions. A point labeled P is placed just above the second row of vectors.

11. Details A vector field and a point are graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. There are five rows of four vectors each. The vectors in the middle row are shorter and become longer as we move up or down. The first three rows from the top have vectors pointing horizontally rightward while the remaining two rows have vectors pointing horizontally leftward. A point labeled P is placed above the space between the second and third vectors in the third row. Zero $${curl}\mathbf{F}$$ points in the negative $$z$$ -direction.

12. Details A vector field and a point are graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The arrows are shorter near the origin and become longer as we move away from the origin in all directions. The vectors seem to trace the path of a family of curves, resembling quarter arcs, that begins from the x axis, going steeply up to the left, and then gradually, and meet the y axis. A point labeled P is placed slightly up and to the right of the center of the vector field.

Recall from Section 14.3 that a function $$g$$ is called harmonic on $$D$$ if it satisfies Laplace’s equation, that is, $$\nabla^{2}g = 0$$ on $$D$$ . Use Green’s first identity (with the same hypotheses as in Exercise 35) to show that if $$g$$ is harmonic on $$D$$ , then $$\oint_{C}{D_{\mathbf{n}}gds = 0}$$ . Here $$D_{\mathbf{n}}g$$ is the normal derivative of $$g$$ defined in Exercise 35.

This exercise demonstrates a connection between the curl vector and rotations. Let $$B$$ be a rigid body rotating about the $$z$$ -axis. The rotation can be described by the vector $$\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{\omega}\mathbf{k}$$ , where $$\omega$$ is the angular speed of $$B$$ , that is, the tangential speed of any point $$P$$ in $$B$$ divided by the distance $$d$$ from the axis of rotation. Let $$\mathbf{r} = {\langle{x,y,z}\rangle}$$ be the position vector of $$P$$ .

list.item: By considering the angle $$\theta$$ in the figure, show that the velocity field of $$B$$ is given by $$\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{w} \times \mathbf{r}$$ .

Show that $${curl}\mathbf{v} = 2\mathbf{w}$$ . Details A three-dimensional rendering of a circular disk, 11 vectors, a line segment, and a curved arrow is graphed in the x y z coordinate plane. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The disk, labeled B, has its center on the positive z-axis. From the center of the top surface of the disk, a vector labeled vector w, rises vertically upward along the positive z axis. A curved arrow around this vector points counterclockwise. From the center of the top surface a short line segment, labeled d, slopes down to the right, perpendicular to the positive z axis, and stops before it reaches the circumference. From its endpoint, a vector labeled vector v, slopes upward to the right, perpendicular to d. From the origin, a vector, labeled P, slopes upward to the right at an angle theta from the positive z-axis, to meet the end point of d and starting point of vector v. Four vectors are tangent to the circumference of the top surface of B. Three vectors are drawn on the top surface of B, perpendicular to the positive z axis, just like vector v.

We have seen that all vector fields of the form $$\mathbf{F} = \nabla g$$ satisfy the equation $${curl}\mathbf{F} = 0$$ and that all vector fields of the form $$\mathbf{F} = {curl}\mathbf{G}$$ satisfy the equation $${div}\mathbf{F} = 0$$ (assuming continuity of the appropriate partial derivatives). This suggests the question: are there any equations that all functions of the form $$f = {div}\mathbf{G}$$ must satisfy? Show that the answer to this question is “no” by proving that every continuous function $$f$$ on $${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ is the divergence of some vector field.
